stem:
A 12-day-old girl has a red left eye with watery discharge and a cluster of vesicles on the left upper eyelid, and has been feeding less well for a day. Fluorescein shows a branching corneal epithelial lesion. She is afebrile and alert. Her mother had painful genital ulcers in the week before a vaginal delivery. The emergency registrar notes that the eye and eyelid are the only obvious sites of disease.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Topical aciclovir and urgent ophthalmology review tomorrow
options.explanation: Topical antiviral treats the cornea but not virus elsewhere; neonatal eye disease can be the first sign of disseminated or CNS infection.

options.label: B
options.text: Oral aciclovir at home, since the disease is limited to the eye
options.explanation: Oral aciclovir is not adequate treatment for neonatal HSV, and apparently localised disease may already involve other organs.

options.label: C
options.text: Swab for culture, start topical chloramphenicol, review in 24 hours
options.explanation: The vesicles, branching corneal lesion and maternal history point to HSV, not bacterial conjunctivitis; waiting a day risks progression.

options.label: D
options.text: IV aciclovir and urgent ophthalmology, deferring LP as she is alert
options.explanation: Being alert does not exclude CNS infection. The CSF result decides the length of treatment, so the LP should be done.

options.label: E
options.text: IV aciclovir, LP with CSF HSV PCR, and urgent ophthalmology
options.explanation: Correct. Neonatal HSV of the skin, eye or mouth needs admission, IV aciclovir and a full work-up including CSF and blood HSV PCR, because CNS or disseminated infection may be present in a well-looking baby; ophthalmology manages the keratitis.

context: Suspected neonatal HSV eye disease needs admission and prompt IV aciclovir, a neonatal infection/HSV work-up and urgent ophthalmology input because ocular disease may accompany systemic or CNS infection.
